items.title: Territorial Acknowledgement
notes: Mayor McCabe opened the meeting with the following Territorial Acknowledgement:

We would like to begin by acknowledging that the land on which we are gathering from today is the land traditionally cared for by the Haudenosaunee, Anishnaabe and Neutral People. We also acknowledge the enduring presence and deep traditional knowledge and philosophies of the Indigenous People with whom we share their land today.

items.title: Moment of Reflection
notes: Mayor McCabe provided Council with a moment of reflection.

January 29 is a solemn day; this year it marked the sixth anniversary of the National Day of Remembrance of the Quebec City Mosque Attack and Action against Islamophobia. Yesterday, the Waterluminate LED lights in Uptown Waterloo were green in recognition of this day.

On January 29, 2017, 6 Muslims - Ibrahima Barry, Mamadou Tanou Barry, Khaled Belkacemi, Abdelkrim Hassane, Azzedine Soufiane, and Aboubaker Thabti were killed and 19 others injured in a hateful act of terror when a person wielding a gun entered the Centre culturel islamique de Québec in Sainte-Foy following evening prayers. This senseless killing was a result of Islamophobia, racism and bigotry.

In memory of the victims, in solidarity with the survivors and those who were injured, the families and friends who lost a loved one, and in recognition of those who put themselves in harm’s way to protect others, we pause, reflect and take action.

This remembrance serves as a critical reminder of the work that must be done to eliminate Islamophobia, hate, racism and all forms of discrimination and prejudice locally and across Canada. A starting point is for residents to join the ongoing Green Square Campaign. The green square represents the green carpets of the Quebec City mosque, where the victims last prayed. It symbolizes that the deceased are believed to spiritually be in a green garden, a better place than their experience the night of the attack.
As a Council we will continue to respond and address all forms of hate and racism in our community.
Mayor McCabe also offered some brief words on Black History Month:

I would like to briefly acknowledge that we are a few days from Black History Month. Events and activities and reflections about Black History Month will start at our next Council Meeting on February 6th, and carry on throughout the month of February.

items.title: Summary of January 10, 2023 Proposed
notes: 2023 Budget Hybrid Public Information Meeting
Report No.: CORP2023-005

Prepared By: Filipa Reynolds, Brad Witzel and Tony Iavarone Daisy Arseneault, Resident of Waterloo and Andre Arseneault, Resident of Waterloo gave a presentation detailing the importance of Active Transportation, national funding strategies that could be utilized for snow clearing, and how snow clearing models tied to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. They also shared words from Stephen Herzog, Resident of Waterloo, regarding how snow got cleared from residential sidewalks, and the potential for Ward-by-Ward snow clearing. They then responded to questions of Council. Filipa Reynolds responded to questions of Council. Mark Dykstra responded to questions of Council.

Eleanor Grant, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the need for sidewalks to get cleared, and the issue with snow plows creating barriers on the sidewalk and at crosswalks. She then responded to questions of Council. Nicole Papke responded to questions of Council. Mark Dykstra responded to questions of Council.

Mason Fitzpatrick, Resident of Waterloo and Sean McCloskey, Resident of Waterloo gave a presentation detailing the different areas of the City where private owners were expected to clear their own sidewalks versus where the City took care of snow removal.
They also compared the City of Waterloo to the City of Guelph’s snow clearing practices and complaints procedure. They then responded to questions of Council.

Janice Jim, Resident of Waterloo, presenting on behalf of Teresa McQuillin, Resident of Waterloo spoke about the need to clear sidewalks from a disability perspective. They then responded to questions of Council.
Mark Dykstra gave an update to the community on the upcoming discussion paper and the impact on the budget.

items.title: 2023-2026 Strategic Plan – Council
notes: Workshop #1
Report No.: CAO2023-010
Prepared By: Sandy Little
Sarah Lewis, Manager, Deloitte, facilitated the “Hot Off the Campaign Trail” workshop and asked each Councillor to share three main themes heard from constituents on the campaign trail.

Councillor Wright wanted to pass her thanks to the residents of Ward 7 who offered their time to share their thoughts. The main themes she heard on the campaign trail were about whether quality of life is eroding and whether we were making the right decisions as a City, access to affordable housing and a mismatch in the supply, and the election process and access to print materials, including meaningful engagement with residents.

Councillor Roe echoed some of Councillor Wright’s comments regarding the election process, and offered the themes she heard on the campaign trail including: affordable housing and homelessness; traffic calming, pedestrian safety and connected systems, such as bike lanes, GRT connections, and trails; and community connectedness and excellence of service from the City, including winter maintenance and leaf collection.

Mayor McCabe shared Councillor Vasic’s three themes on her behalf: traffic calming, safety and ease of mobility, including winter accessibility concerns; housing and homelessness; and covid-19 recovery, including supporting small businesses, a general lack of connectedness, and an enhanced arts and culture sector.

Councillor Freeman shared the main themes heard on her campaign: traffic and traffic speeds, specifically that they are not supportive of 30km/h speed limits; climate change and continuing to move forward with important efforts; and diversity, equity and inclusion, including how individuals are recognized in programs and intake forms, the opportunity to build a Reconciliation Contribution fund, and the role of the city within housing and homelessness.

Councillor Roach also echoed Councillor Roe and Councillor Wright as far as the election went, mentioning that there was a lot of election fatigue. The three main themes heard on his campaign were: affordable housing, including the price of rent; traffic concerns, with specific mention to the roundabouts in Conservation Meadows; and city services such as leaf collection and snow clearing.

Councillor Bodaly shared some of the different concerns he heard while campaigning, and offered the main themes: safe streets, including how to make streets safer for pedestrians, cyclists, seniors, and youth; what the City is doing surrounding climate change; affordable housing, including homelessness and affordable units; and equity and inclusion, including a sense of belonging by the community.

Councillor Hanmer shared the main themes from her campaign: affordable housing, including appropriate rents and the “missing middle”; traffic calming measures, including 30km/h speed limits around school zones and issues with the roundabout at Ira Needles and Erb; active transportation and the connections across the City; and park maintenance, which may have fallen to the wayside during the pandemic.

Mayor McCabe shared some of the concerns she heard on the campaign trail, as well as the main themes: affordable and attainable housing; traffic and road safety, including that many residents don’t want the speed reduced; climate change, including the need for climate friendly new builds; and community connectedness, and finding a sense of purpose within the community.

Sarah Lewis, Manager, Deloitte, continued her presentation and led Council through the next steps of the Strategic Planning stages. Sandy Little shared information on the Strategic Plan preparation steps.
